title: Summer at a roof garden near Shreveport; church music
summary: Charles recalls a summer job and living at Dr. King's house; Brown talks about piano in Protestant churches.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: time, you know. You're from around Shreveport? Yes, north of Shreveport. Well, I played over there because you were in a roof garden for a whole summer, for Mr. Ballantyne. Sure. He came and got me, I was playing that tomass in there. That's right. That's right. A whole summer I played that. Oh but that was one of the best roof garden jobs I ever had. Oh that was a nice place. Oh, we used to live at Dr. King's house on Douglas Street. I used to go to, on Sundays I used to go to the Protestant church. They had a Catholic church there but I don't think they had a handful of

people there. Oh, in those days there were relatively few Catholics there. That's right. That's right. Did they have any jazzy piano playing and jazzy music at the Protestant church you attended? No. Well I was raised up, for instance, going to both white churches and also Negro churches up there. They had some very gut-buckety piano playing, you know, rather goofy piano playing in the churches. There was one girl who, named Jewel Webb, who had learned it from listening to the records of the Economist who played for Bessie Smith. And when she went to the Baptist church in Mansfield, the second Baptist church, I was saying, oh Mansfield, boy you really heard some down-to-earth piano playing in those Protestant hymns. Is there anything that you have neglected on this thing here?
